learn: Every sound is made when something vibrates. To vibrate means to move back and forth very fast.
When you pluck a rubber band, it shakes and you hear a twang.
Put your fingers on your throat and hum. You can feel your voice box vibrate.
lessons.try: Hum with your fingers on your throat, then stop. What do you feel?

learn: Sometimes you can see vibrations.
Put rice on a drum and tap it. The rice jumps.
A tuning fork dipped in water makes the water splash.
check: What happens to rice on a tapped drum?
A tuning fork in water makes the water...
lessons.try: Stretch plastic wrap over a bowl, put grains of rice on top, and hum near it.

learn: Big vibrations make loud sounds. Small vibrations make soft sounds.
Fast vibrations make high sounds. Slow vibrations make low sounds.
A thin, tight string sounds higher than a thick, loose one.
check: Big vibrations make sounds that are...
Fast vibrations make sounds that are...
lessons.try: Pluck a tight rubber band and a loose one. Which is higher?

learn: We see things when light bounces off them and goes into our eyes.
In a completely dark room, we cannot see anything.
Light can come from the Sun, lamps, fire and flashlights.
check: What do we need to see?
In a completely dark room we can see...
lessons.try: Look at a toy in a bright room, then in a very dark closet. What changes?

learn: Things that make their own light are light sources.
The Sun, a candle and a light bulb are light sources.
The Moon is not a light source. It shines because sunlight bounces off it.
check: Is a candle a light source?
lessons.try: List three light sources in your home.

learn: A shadow forms when something blocks light.
Light travels in straight lines, so it cannot go around objects.
Move a flashlight closer to an object and the shadow gets bigger.
check: Flashlight closer to an object makes the shadow...
lessons.try: Make shadow animals with your hands and a flashlight.

learn: Transparent materials let almost all light through. You can see clearly through them.
Clear glass, clean water and plastic wrap are transparent.
Windows are made of transparent glass so light can come in.
lessons.try: Shine a flashlight through a clear glass of water.

learn: Translucent materials let some light through, but you cannot see clearly. Wax paper and tissue paper are translucent.
Opaque materials let no light through. Wood, cardboard and metal are opaque.
Opaque objects make the darkest shadows.
lessons.try: Test a sock, wax paper and a plastic bag with a flashlight. Sort them.

learn: A mirror is very smooth and shiny. It bounces light back. This is called reflection.
You can use a mirror to send light around a corner.
Shiny things like spoons and still water reflect too.
check: What does a mirror do to light?
What is it called when light bounces back?
lessons.try: With a grown-up, use a mirror to bounce flashlight light onto a wall.

units.t: Sending Messages with Light and Sound

learn: People have always used light and sound to send messages far away.
Drums could send messages from village to village.
Lighthouses shine light to warn ships about rocks.
check: What do lighthouses warn ships about?
It is time to change activities
lessons.try: Think of a sound that tells you something, like a school bell.

learn: A code uses patterns to stand for words.
Morse code uses short and long signals: dots and dashes. SOS is three short, three long, three short.
You can send code with a flashlight or by tapping.
lessons.try: Make up a code with a friend: one tap means yes, two taps means no.

learn: Engineers design tools to solve problems, like talking over a distance.
A cup telephone uses a string. Your voice vibrates the string, and the vibration travels to the other cup.
The string must be tight for it to work.
check: What travels along a cup telephone string?
Who designs tools to solve problems?
lessons.try: With a grown-up, make a cup telephone with two paper cups and a long string.

learn: Roots hold the plant in the ground and drink water and nutrients from the soil.
The stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves.
Celery is a stem you can eat. Carrots are roots.
check: Drink water and hold the plant
Carries water and holds the plant up
lessons.try: Put a celery stalk in coloured water and watch it over a day.

learn: Leaves use sunlight, air and water to make food for the plant.
Most leaves are flat and wide to catch lots of sunlight.
Lettuce and spinach are leaves we eat.
check: Why are most leaves flat and wide?
lessons.try: Collect three different leaves and compare their shapes.

learn: Flowers help plants make seeds. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.
Fruits hold and protect seeds. An apple has seeds inside.
A seed can grow into a new plant.
check: What can a seed grow into?
lessons.try: Cut open a fruit with a grown-up and count the seeds.

learn: Animals have body parts that help them move.
Birds have wings to fly. Fish have fins to swim. Frogs have strong back legs to jump.
Each part fits where the animal lives.
lessons.try: Act out how three animals move.

learn: Animals have body parts that help them get food.
An eagle has a sharp beak to tear meat. A hummingbird has a long thin beak to sip nectar.
A giraffe's long neck helps it reach leaves high in trees.
check: What helps a giraffe reach high leaves?
A long thin beak is good for...
What do eagles use to tear meat?
lessons.try: Look at pictures of bird beaks. Guess what each bird eats.

learn: Some body parts keep animals safe.
A turtle has a hard shell. A porcupine has sharp quills.
Some animals have colours that help them hide, called camouflage.
check: Colours that help an animal hide
lessons.try: Draw an animal that is hiding with camouflage.

learn: People get ideas for inventions by looking at plants and animals. This is called biomimicry.
Hook-and-loop fasteners were invented after a man noticed burrs sticking to his dog's fur.
Swim flippers copy the webbed feet of ducks and frogs.
check: What gave the idea for hook-and-loop fasteners?
lessons.try: Look at a burr or a seed with hooks under a magnifying glass, or look at a picture.

learn: A bike helmet has a hard outside, like a turtle's shell.
Some buildings stay cool like termite mounds, which have air tunnels.
Raincoats keep water off like a duck's oily feathers.
check: A bike helmet is like a...
A raincoat keeps water off like...
lessons.try: Find something at home that works like an animal body part.

learn: Engineers ask a question, imagine ideas, make a plan, build it and test it.
You can solve a problem by copying a plant or animal.
For example, to stay warm, copy a polar bear's thick fur.
check: What do engineers do after they build?
To stay warm, you could copy...
What is the first step in design?
lessons.try: Design a tool that helps you pick up things, copying a bird's beak.

learn: Young animals and plants are like their parents in many ways.
A kitten looks like a cat. A puppy looks like a dog.
But they are not exactly the same. Puppies in one litter can have different colours.
check: Are babies exactly like their parents?
Can puppies in one litter look different?
lessons.try: Look at photos of baby and adult animals and match them.

learn: Some young animals look very different from their parents.
A caterpillar becomes a butterfly. A tadpole becomes a frog.
As they grow, they change shape.
check: Do some animals change shape as they grow?
lessons.try: Draw the life of a frog: egg, tadpole, frog.

learn: Many animal parents help their babies survive.
Birds feed their chicks. Kangaroos carry joeys in a pouch.
Wolves teach their pups to hunt. Some animals, like sea turtles, do not stay with their young.
check: Where does a kangaroo carry its baby?
What do birds do for their chicks?
Do all animals stay with their young?
lessons.try: Name one way human parents help their children.

learn: The Sun seems to rise in the east in the morning and set in the west in the evening.
The Sun is not really moving across the sky. Earth is spinning.
Never look straight at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes.
check: Where does the Sun seem to rise?
Why does the Sun seem to move?
Should you look straight at the Sun?
lessons.try: Mark where the Sun is in the morning and afternoon from the same window.

learn: The Moon looks different on different nights.
Sometimes it is full and round. Sometimes it is a thin crescent. Sometimes we cannot see it.
The pattern repeats about every month. These shapes are called phases.
check: What are the Moon's shapes called?
About how long does the Moon's pattern take?
A thin curved Moon is called a...
lessons.try: Draw the Moon every clear night for a week.

learn: Stars are giant balls of hot, glowing gas very far away.
The Sun is a star. It is the closest star to Earth.
We see stars at night because the sky is dark. They are still there in the day.
check: What is the closest star to Earth?
Why do we see stars at night?
They only come out at night
lessons.try: On a clear night, count the stars you can see in one patch of sky.

learn: The four seasons are spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter.
Summer is warmest. Winter is coldest.
The seasons repeat every year.
check: Do the seasons repeat every year?
lessons.try: Draw a tree in each season.

learn: In summer, there are more hours of daylight. The Sun sets late.
In winter, there are fewer hours of daylight. It gets dark early.
Spring and autumn are in between.
lessons.try: Write down what time it gets dark tonight. Check again in a month.

learn: Scientists record sunrise and sunset times to find patterns.
A chart can show how many hours of daylight each month has.
Patterns help us predict what will happen next.
check: What do patterns help us do?
lessons.try: Look up today's sunrise and sunset times with a grown-up.
